mentl/48940de:
Corrects the previous pin, which shipped a broken incremental compile.

f58dfc10 moved module identity onto the resolved path and took the tree scan
and manifest with it, but split_weave_by_module still bucketed analyzed
statements by NAME. assoc_stmts answered EMPTY for every cached module, so
the warm path emitted the cone alone — 2933 bytes against a cold compile's
37644, the whole restored program dropped.

It rode a pin because the frontier's warm-inc leg returns on its first
failure. The cone-line check went red on a rendering change (the cone prints
paths now, being the identity it carries) and the byte-compare below it —
the check that catches exactly this bug — never ran.

Two fixes, and the second is the one that matters: the bucket keys on the
range tuple's path (range_of_module keeps the name, which is what a user
types at an address), and the leg no longer returns on an independent
failure. A leg that halts at its first red hides the rest of its own
coverage.

Also: the census leg keeps its children's stderr and exit codes, so a query
that dies is no longer reported as a missing shape — a diagnostic whose name
could lie, inside the gate built to catch those.

perennials/48f7ce6:
The server ships plants sorted by documentation richness, a global
signal with no regional pull, so a tropical that dies in a zone-6
winter outranked a serviceberry whenever contributors wrote more about
it. The dataset now assembles banded by a remembered home zone
(perennials.zone.v1, seeded 6, re-learned whenever she names a zone in
a search or applies a spot): recorded-hardy first, unmeasured in the
middle, recorded misfits last, richness still deciding within a band.
It is an order, not a filter, and a plant nobody measured never ranks
below one the record says dies there. The home store opts out of
cross-tab sync: a zone named in one tab must not reorder and truncate
a list another tab is scrolled deep into; other tabs pick the new zone
up when they next assemble the dataset. The text index survives the
re-sort, since it never cared about order.
